en: The Dharma Gate of the Merits of the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ocean-like Marks of Amitābha Buddha,
compiled and recorded by the Bhikṣu Shandao, in one fascicle.

I. The Method for Contemplating the Buddha through Samādhi according to the *Amitābha Sūtra*. II. The Method for Mindfulness of the Buddha through Samādhi according to the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*. III. The Method for Entering the Ritual Site (*maṇḍala*) and Practicing Mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Sūtras. IV. The Method for Repentance and Making Vows within the Ritual Site according to the Sūtras. Regarding the first section, "The Method for Contemplating the Buddha through Samādhi according to the *Amitābha Sūtra*": Based on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, one contemplates the Buddha’s body as being of true golden color, with a circular halo that shines through all, and a countenance of incomparable excellence. This is derived from the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, and the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitābha Buddha*.
Practitioners and others should always, at all times and in all places, day and night, constantly maintain this visualization.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they should likewise maintain this visualization.
At all times, they should remain with their minds directed toward the west.
One should understand that the various signs, such as the adornments of all kinds of jewels belonging to those noble assemblies,
appear as if they were right before one's eyes.
Furthermore, when a practitioner wishes to sit,
they must first assume the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*):
place the left foot upon the right thigh so that it is level with the outer edge.
The right foot is placed upon the left thigh so that it aligns with the outer edge;
the right hand is placed within the palm of the left hand,
with the two thumbs touching face-to-face.
Next, straighten the body and sit upright;
close the mouth and close the eyes so that they appear neither open nor closed,
neither shut nor unshut.
He immediately used his mind’s eye to observe from above, starting from the Buddha’s cranial protuberance;
the scalp appeared golden in color,
and the hair was a deep azure-blue.
Each hair curls like a conch shell atop his head.
His skull is the color of snow, transparent inside and out;
his brain is the color of crystal.
Next, visualize that there are fourteen channels within the brain;
each channel has fourteen rays of light which emerge outward from the pores at the roots of the hair.
The coiled hair winds around seven times,
then returns and enters through the pore at the tip of the hair.
Next, visualize the aforementioned light emerging from the pores at the roots of the two eyebrows and extending outward.
Next, visualize the mark of the broad and level forehead.
Next, visualize the mark of the high and long eyebrows, which are like the crescent moon.
Next, visualize the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, coiled in the space between them.
Its hairs are white, solid on the outside and hollow within;
they emit golden light that issues forth from the tips of the hairs.
Directly observe your own body,
as stated in the *Buddhadhyānasamādhisūtra*:
"If there is a person..."
If one contemplates the mark of the white tuft for even a single moment—
whether it is seen or not—
one shall immediately eliminate the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over ninety-six billion nayutas of Ganges-sand particles of kalpas.
Constantly maintaining this contemplation will greatly eliminate obstacles and extinguish transgressions,
and one will further attain immeasurable merit.
All the Buddhas rejoice.
Next, visualize the two eyes as broad and long, with black and white clearly distinguished, their radiance shining through with penetrating clarity.
Next, visualize the nose as long, high, and straight, like a cast gold ingot.
Next, visualize the face as level and full, without any protrusions or depressions.
Next, visualize the earlobes hanging down,
with seven hairs in each pore from which light radiates.
Visualize the Buddha’s body as all-pervadingly radiant.
Next, visualize the color of his lips as a beautiful red, luminous and glossy.
Next, visualize his teeth as white, even, and closely set.
White as a conch or the moon,
it is translucent both inside and out.
Next, visualize the tongue as thin, broad, long, and soft.
Beneath the tongue-root are two channels;
the津液 (tīng-yè, nutritive fluids) flow into the pharynx and enter directly into the heart-king.
The Buddha-mind is like a red lotus flower;
it neither opens nor closes, yet it neither remains open nor closed.
It possesses eighty-four thousand petals.
The leaves are layered one upon another;
each leaf has eighty-four thousand veins,
and each vein has eighty-four thousand rays of light.
Each ray of light becomes a lotus flower made of a hundred jewels;
upon each flower sits a bodhisattva of the tenth stage,
their bodies all golden in color.
Holding incense and flowers in their hands, they make offerings to the Mind-King;
with one voice and in unison, they sing praises to the Mind-King.
When the practitioners form this visualization, [they should proceed as follows].
One eliminates karmic obstacles and attains immeasurable merit;
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rejoice,
as do the devas, spirits, and ghosts.
Again, draw the heart upward.
Next, visualize the circular marks at the throat and the back of the neck, as well as the circular marks on the two shoulders.
Next, visualize the rounded and muscular form of the two arms.
Next, visualize that the palms of both hands are flat and full, marked with the sign of the thousand-spoked wheel;
the ten fingers are slender and long, joined by webbing between them,
and the nails have the color of red copper.
Again, draw the heart upward.
Next, visualize the mark of the chest being level and full, with the syllable of the ten thousand virtues appearing clearly before the Buddha’s breast.
Next, visualize the mark of the abdomen being level and not protruding.
Next, one should visualize the circular navel cavity as having a deep appearance, with its inner and outer surfaces constantly illuminated by light.
Next, one should visualize the male organ (kośagata-vyañjana) as perfectly full,
like the moon on the night of the fifteenth day.
It is also like the belly and the back;
in their flatness, there is no distinction.
The Buddha said:
If there are men or women who have much craving for sensual forms,
they should immediately bring to mind the Tathāgata’s mark of the concealed male organ.
The lustful mind immediately ceases;
karmic obstructions are eliminated and extinguished, and one attains immeasurable merit.
All Buddhas rejoice.
Devas and spirits will protect you with benevolent hearts;
you shall enjoy long life, peace, and happiness, forever free from illness.
Next, visualize that both thighs and knees are perfectly rounded.
Next, visualize the two lower legs as being like the haunches of a deer king.
Next, visualize the two heels as being like the trunks of an elephant king.
Next, visualize the two insteps as being as high as the shells of a tortoise king.
Next, visualize that the ten toes of the feet are long and have webbing between them,
with the nails the color of red copper.
Next, visualize the Buddha seated in the full lotus posture.
Place the left foot upon the right thigh so that it aligns with its outer edge;
place the right foot upon the left thigh so that it aligns with its outer edge.
Next, visualize that beneath both feet there are the marks of thousand-spoked wheels.
The spokes and the rim are complete,
all emitting light that shines universally throughout the lands of the ten directions.
From the crown of his head down to his feet, he possesses the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel.
This is called "being fully endowed with the merit of the adornments of the Buddha’s form-body," and it is termed "sequential contemplation.
Next, one should visualize the method for the flower seat.
Next, visualize the appearance of the flower pedestal.
Next, visualize the flower petals;
they are layered one upon another in eighty-four thousand tiers.
On each and every leaf, one should visualize a billion jewel-kings as adornments.
Within each jewel are eighty-four thousand rays of light,
which shine upward upon the Buddha’s body.
Next, visualize the stem of the jewel-flower as having eight facets;
each facet is adorned with hundreds of thousands of various jewels and emits great radiance,
illuminating both above and below.
Next, visualize that the stem of the flower rests upon the jeweled ground.
From the various jewels upon the ground, eighty-four thousand rays of light are emitted,
each ray illuminating the Buddha’s body.
Furthermore, one visualizes the ten directions and the six realms of existence,
imagining that all these lights come to touch and illumine one's own body.
While forming this visualization:
One eliminates karmic obstacles and attains immeasurable merit;
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rejoice,
and the devas and spirits likewise rejoice.
Day and night, following like a shadow, they shall protect the practitioner.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they shall always attain peace and security.
They shall enjoy long life, wealth, and happiness, forever free from illness and pain.
In accordance with Buddhism,
one may come to see the phenomena within the Pure Land; however,
if one sees them, they are known only to oneself.
One must not speak of this to others;
to do so incurs great sin and brings about the retribution of sudden illness and a short life.
This applies unless one follows the teachings of the Dharma-gate.
At the time of death,
one will be reborn in the highest grade in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Thus, one should perform the aforementioned sixteenfold contemplation repeatedly, both upward and downward.
Thereafter, settle the mind upon the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
One must strictly restrain the mind to keep it upright;
it must not be allowed to become distracted or confused again.
One will immediately lose the concentrated mind;
it should be known that samādhi is difficult to achieve.
This is called the method for contemplating the Buddha through the Samādhi of Contemplation.
At all times, one should constantly dedicate [merit] toward rebirth in the Pure Land,
relying solely on the "settling of the mind" according to the thirteen contemplations of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
"You shall certainly attain it, without doubt.
He further addressed the practitioner, saying,
"I wish to be born in the Pure Land."
One need only maintain the precepts, recite the Buddha's name,
and chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* fifteen times daily;
in two years, one will have completed ten thousand recitations.
Thirty times per day;
ten thousand times per year.
Recite the Buddha’s name ten thousand times each day.
One must also, according to the proper time, perform prostrations and praises to the adornments of the Pure Land.
Those who apply themselves with great diligence— whether they attain thirty thousand, sixty thousand, or one hundred thousand [recitations]—
are all those destined for the highest grade of the highest birth.
One should know that all remaining merits are dedicated entirely toward rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Thus far,
the method for the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha has been explained.

From the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, Chapter on Questions: The Method of Entering the Dharma-Assembly for Seven Days and Seven Nights to Practice the Buddha-Mindfulness Samādhi. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla: [The method of entering the dharma-assembly for seven days and seven nights to practice the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi, as set forth in the Chapter on Questions of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
There is a samādhi named "All Buddhas of the Ten Directions Standing Before One.
One who can practice this dharma [attains it].
"What you have asked can all be attained.
Bhadrapāla said to the Buddha,
"I pray that you will explain it for me."
He delivers many across [suffering],
bringing peace and security to the ten directions,
and manifests a great sign of illumination for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"There is a samādhi named 'concentration of the mind'."
A student should always maintain and practice this;
they must not follow other teachings again.
This is the foremost among all merits.
The next chapter, "On Practice," states:
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to quickly attain this samādhi..."
If one constantly establishes great faith and practices according to the Dharma,
then it can be attained.
Do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of doubt.
This method for the concentrated mind is called "The Bodhisattva’s Transcendence of All Practices.
Establish a single moment of thought; have faith in this Dharma; according to what you have heard, be mindful of its direction.
One should, with a single thought, sever all conceptualizations; establish firm faith and do not harbor doubt.
Practice with vigor and do not be indolent. Do not give rise to thoughts, and do not dwell on existence or non-existence.
Do not think of advancing, do not think of retreating, do not think of what is before, and do not think of what is behind.
Do not think of the left; do not think of the right; do not think of non-existence; do not think of existence;
do not think of the distant; do not think of the near; do not think of pain; do not think of itching;
do not think of hunger; do not think of thirst; do not think of cold; do not think of heat.
Do not dwell on suffering; do not dwell on pleasure. Do not dwell on birth; do not dwell on old age.
Do not dwell on illness; do not dwell on death. Do not dwell on life; do not dwell on longevity.
Do not dwell on poverty; do not dwell on wealth. Do not dwell on nobility; do not dwell on lowliness.
Do not dwell on form; do not dwell on desire; do not dwell on the small;
do not dwell on the large; do not dwell on the long; do not dwell on the short; do not dwell on the beautiful;
do not dwell on the ugly; do not dwell on the evil; do not dwell on the good; do not dwell on anger; do not dwell on joy.
Do not dwell on sitting; do not dwell on rising; do not dwell on walking;
do not dwell on stopping. Do not dwell on sutras; do not dwell on dharmas; do not dwell on "is";
do not dwell on "is not. Do not dwell on relinquishing; do not dwell on grasping; do not dwell on perception; do not dwell on consciousness.
Do not contemplate cessation; do not contemplate attachment; do not contemplate emptiness; do not contemplate reality.
Do not contemplate lightness; do not contemplate heaviness; do not contemplate difficulty; do not contemplate ease. Do not contemplate depth;
do not contemplate shallowness; do not contemplate breadth; do not contemplate narrowness.
Do not dwell on your father; do not dwell on your mother; do not dwell on your wife; do not dwell on your children; do not dwell on your kin;
do not dwell on those who are distant; do not dwell on the hateful; do not dwell on the beloved;
do not dwell on gain; do not dwell on loss; do not dwell on success; do not dwell on failure.
Do not dwell on purity; do not dwell on turbidity. Sever all thoughts.
For the duration of this single lifetime, let the mind not be distracted. Always be diligent; do not calculate by the year, nor grow weary by the day.
Establish a single thought and do not be negligent midway. Eliminate sleep and refine your intention.
Always dwell alone; do not gather in crowds. Avoid evil people and draw near to virtuous friends and a wise teacher.
Regard them as the Buddha, uphold their resolve, and always remain gentle.
Contemplate equality toward all things. Avoid your native village and distance yourself from your kinsmen.
Abandoning craving and desire, treading the path of purity, practicing non-action, and severing all lusts;
casting aside distracted thoughts, cultivating meditative concentration, and training in wisdom— thus one must, through dhyāna,
eliminate the three defilements, remove the six sense bases, cut off sensual passion, and detach from all attachments.
Do not covet wealth; do not hoard it in abundance. Be moderate in eating; do not crave flavors. Do not take the lives of sentient beings;
be careful not to eat [meat]. Wear robes according to the Dharma; do not adorn yourself with finery.
Do not engage in frivolous play; do not be arrogant; do not be conceited; do not be haughty.
If one expounds the sutras, one should do so in accordance with the Dharma: Realize that the body is fundamentally like an illusion;
Do not grasp at the aggregates (*skandha*), And do not enter into the elements (*dhātu*). The aggregates are like thieves, And the four [elements] are like snakes.
They are impermanent, They are evanescent, They have no permanent master, And are realized to be fundamentally non-existent.
When causes and conditions assemble, and when causes and conditions disperse— fully understanding this, one knows they are fundamentally non-existent.
Extending compassion to all, giving to the poor and destitute,
and rescuing those who do not turn back— this is the samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s practice, the essential wisdom that transcends all other deeds.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"By maintaining these practices,
you shall immediately attain samādhi."
All the Buddhas of the present now stand before them.
Should there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who practice in accordance with the Dharma, [they shall be protected].
Maintaining the precepts in their entirety,
one dwells alone in a solitary place,
mindful that Amitābha Buddha is currently residing in the Western Quarter.
You should keep in mind what you have heard:
ten million billion buddha-fields away from here is a land named Sukhāvatī.
Focus your mind on this single-mindedly for one day and night, or seven days and seven nights.
After the seven days have passed, you will see it.
It is, for example, like what one sees in a dream:
one does not know day from night, nor does one know the internal from the external;
it is not because of being obscured by darkness that one does not see.
Bhadra, when the fourfold assembly constantly forms this thought,
within the realm of the Buddhas there are great mountains, such as Mount Sumeru.
All dark and obscure places were opened up for them, free from any obstruction or hindrance.
This was because these four assemblies did not rely on the divine eye to see through,
nor did they rely on the divine ear to hear through.
Without employing supernormal powers to reach that buddha-field,
and without passing away from this world to be reborn there,
he beholds it while remaining seated right here.
The Buddha said:
"The fourfold assembly in this world-system, by recollecting Amitābha Buddha with single-minded devotion,
shall succeed in seeing him."
He immediately asked, "By practicing what dharma can one be born in this land?
Amitābha Buddha replied,
"Those who wish to come and be born here should keep my name in mind."
Without ceasing for a moment,
they immediately attain rebirth.
The Buddha said:
Through single-minded mindfulness, one attains rebirth there,

constantly recollecting the Buddha’s body with its thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary characteristics, its billions of rays of light shining through all things, its peerless beauty, and its preaching of the Dharma amidst the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Do not destroy form.
Why? Because form is indestructible.
Because one recollects the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya),
one attains this samādhi.
The above clarifies the method for the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.
When wishing to enter the maṇḍala of samādhi,
one must first prepare the maṇḍala according to the methods taught by the Buddha.
Install the sacred image and sprinkle it with fragrant water for cleansing;
if there is no Buddha hall, [perform this elsewhere].
It is also permissible to use a clean room;
one should sweep and sprinkle it according to the ritual rules,
and install a single Buddha image on the western wall.
The practitioners [should practice] from the first day of the month to the eighth,
or from the eighth to the fifteenth,
or from the fifteenth to the twenty-third.
Alternatively, from the twenty-third day to the thirtieth day,
these four periods each month are auspicious.
Practitioners and others should weigh their own domestic responsibilities accordingly.
During this time, one enters the path of pure practice;
whether for one day or up to seven days,
one must wear clean robes throughout.
One's shoes and sandals must also be new and clean.
For seven days, one must observe the long fast, eating only once a day.
Soft cakes and coarse rice, along with seasonings and vegetables, should be frugal and measured according to the occasion.
Within the place of practice, one should bind the mind continuously day and night,
single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha,
with the mind and the voice proceeding in uninterrupted succession.
One should remain only sitting or standing;
for seven days, one must not sleep,
nor is it necessary to perform prostrations to the Buddha or recite sutras at fixed times.
One need not even hold a rosary.
It is sufficient simply to know how to join the palms and recite the Buddha’s name, maintaining in every thought the visualization of seeing the Buddha.
Thus the Buddha said.
One should bring to mind Amitābha Buddha’s body of true golden color, its radiance shining through all, and its incomparable, upright beauty,
as if it were present before one's eyes.
While thus recollecting the Buddha:
If standing, one should immediately maintain mindfulness for ten thousand or twenty thousand [breaths].
If sitting, one should sit and maintain mindfulness for ten thousand or twenty thousand [breaths].
Within the site of practice, one must not turn heads to converse in secret.
Day and night, or at three or six periods,
one should declare before all Buddhas, all worthy sages, and the officials of the celestial and terrestrial courts,
confessing and repenting for all the various offenses committed through body, speech, and mind throughout one's entire life.
Having performed the confession according to the actual facts,
one should subsequently return to recollecting the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma;
whatever visions or realms one perceives must not be spoken of rashly.
Those who are virtuous shall know this for themselves;
those who have committed evil shall repent.
They vow to abstain from alcohol, meat, and the five pungent roots.
Do not grasp with the hands; do not eat with the mouth.
If you violate these words, may both body and mouth be afflicted with malignant sores.
Alternatively, one may vow to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times in total,
reciting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times daily,
and reciting the sūtra fifteen times each day.
Recite it twenty or thirty times,
according to one's capacity;
vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
May the Buddha graciously accept this.
Furthermore, whether practitioners are ill or healthy, when they are about to pass away,
they should rely solely upon the aforementioned method of the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
With body and mind properly aligned,
turn the face toward the west,
and let the mind likewise remain focused.
Visualize Amitābha Buddha;
let your mind and speech correspond so that the sound does not cease for a moment.
Form the firm resolve to be reborn there, and imagine the holy assembly coming to welcome you upon the lotus pedestal.
If the patient sees an object before him,
he should immediately speak of it to the attendant;
once the attendant has heard what was said, [he should act accordingly].
This is recorded according to the oral instructions.
Furthermore, if the patient is unable to speak,
the caregiver must repeatedly ask the patient what kind of visions they are seeing.
If the nature of the offense is described,
bystanders will immediately recite the Buddha’s name and assist in the collective repentance.
They shall certainly cause their transgressions to be extinguished.
If their transgressions are extinguished,
the holy assembly upon the flower pedestal will appear before them in accordance with their thoughts.
According to the previous commentary and records:
furthermore, when practitioners or their relatives and six kinds of kin come to visit the sick,
do not allow those who consume food, alcohol, meat, or the five pungent vegetables to enter.
If one must not go near a sick person,
one will immediately lose right mindfulness,
and malevolent spirits and ghosts will cause confusion.
The patient died of madness and fell into the three evil realms.
May practitioners alike exercise great self-restraint and uphold the Buddha’s teachings,
so that we may together create the causes and conditions for seeing the Buddha.
The above constitutes the ritual procedures for entering the *maṇḍala* and for attending to the sick.

Based on the scriptures, there are six sections clarifying the meaning of the five kinds of sovereign conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*): 1. Based on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*. 2. Based on the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*. 3. Based on the four-fascicle *Amitābha-sūtra*. 4. Based on the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*. 5. Based on the *Daśavihāra-sūtra*. 6. Based on the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-samādhi-sūtra*. I have respectfully relied upon these six sūtras concerning rebirth, in accordance with the teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha.
It clarifies that those who recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land shall,
in this very life, obtain increased longevity and avoid the calamities of the nine untimely deaths.
Each point is fully explained as set forth in the "Meaning of the Five Conditions" below. Question:
The Buddha exhorts all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta.
One should vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Amitābha Buddha;
furthermore, one should encourage the creation of images of Amitābha,
and offer praise, prostrations, incense, and flowers as offerings.
Day and night, he practiced visualization without ceasing;
furthermore, he exhorted others to single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten thousand,
twenty thousand, thirty thousand, or fifty thousand times.
As for those who reach up to one hundred thousand recitations,
some are encouraged to chant the Amitābha Sūtra fifteen,
twenty-three, thirty-five, or fifty times.
As for those who reach one hundred times ten thousand recitations,
what merit will they obtain in this present life?
And after they relinquish their report at the end of a hundred years?
"What benefit is there?
Will one be reborn in the Pure Land or not?
He replied:
In this present life and at the time of casting off the body, there will certainly be great merit and benefit.
Based on the Buddha’s teachings, five kinds of superior causal conditions for benefit are clearly elucidated.
The first is the superior condition for the extinction of offenses.
Second, the superior condition of being protected by mindfulness so as to attain long life;
third, the superior condition of seeing the Buddha;
fourth, the superior condition of gathering in sentient beings.
Fifth is the dominant condition for the realization of birth.
Regarding the dominant condition for the extinction of offenses, this refers,
for example, to those born in the highest grade of the lowest level according to the *Amitābha-sūtra* (the *Contemplation Sūtra*).
Suppose there is a person who has committed the ten grave evils throughout their entire life.
When that person falls ill and is on the verge of death,
they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who instructs them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha even once.
This immediately eliminates the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas;
it serves as a superior condition for the eradication of offenses within this very life.
Furthermore, it is like those born as humans of the lower grade.
Throughout one's entire life, one has committed offenses against the Buddha-dharma,
violated the precepts and the fast,
and consumed the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Feeling no shame or remorse,
that person falls ill and is on the verge of death;
then, the various fires of hell arrive all at once.
Upon encountering a virtuous friend who explains for them the physical marks and features of Amitābha Buddha, his merits and virtues, and the adornments of his land,
the sinner, having heard this,
immediately eliminates the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
The hells are immediately extinguished.
This is also a superior condition for the extinction of offenses within the present life.
Furthermore, it is like those who attain rebirth in the lower grade of the lowest level.
Throughout one's life, having committed the five heinous and most grave offenses,
one undergoes endless suffering while passing through the hells; then,
the offender falls ill and is on the verge of death.
Upon encountering a virtuous friend who instructs one to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times,
within each and every utterance, the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas are extinguished.
This is also a superior condition for the extinction of offenses in the present life.
Furthermore, if there is someone who,
relying on the *Amitābha Sūtra* and other texts, creates a transformation of the adornments of the Pure Land and contemplates and visualizes the jeweled ground day and night.
In this present life, one eradicates, moment by moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
Furthermore, according to the sūtra,
one should paint a transformation tableau and perform visualization meditation on the adornments of jeweled trees, jeweled ponds, and jeweled pavilions.
In this present life, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Furthermore, for those who rely on the adornment of the lotus seat and practice visualization day and night,
they eliminate the sins of birth and death of fifty billion kalpas in every thought-moment of this present life.
Furthermore, by relying on the sutras to practice the visualization of the imagined body, the true body, and the visualizations of Avalokiteśvara,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others, one will, in every moment of the present life, eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable billions of kalpas.
As cited above,
these are all the predominant conditions for the eradication of offenses in the present life.
Furthermore, regarding what is called the "predominant condition of protective mindfulness":
As it is said in the twelfth contemplation:
"If there is a person who,
at all times and in all places, day and night, contemplates with a sincere mind the two-fold retributive adornments of Amitābha’s Pure Land."
Whether they see it or not,
Amitāyus Buddha manifests countless transformation Buddhas,
and Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta likewise manifest countless transformation bodies.
They constantly come to this place where practitioners reside;
they are also a superior condition for protection and mindfulness in this present life.
Furthermore, as stated in the latter part of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:
If there is anyone who,
with a sincere heart, constantly keeps in mind Amitābha Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas,

Again, he thought:
"The World-Honored One possesses great compassion and responds universally to all.
If this merit of mine is granted, I shall be spared from sinking forever into the ocean of suffering."
"The Tathāgata shall appear and preach the Dharma for me.
Driven by this aspiration and longing, the king did not eat for three days.
The Buddha then manifested his form and, together with the assembly of noble ones, entered the palace.
I preached the Dharma for the king.
Furthermore, by this proof,
it is evident that the king’s mind is truly authentic.
As each thought-moment removes obstacles,
the Buddha knows that their transgressions have been extinguished and appears before them in accordance with their thoughts.
